summary: This note is a encyclopedic-style overview of infidelity, defined as a violation of a couple's emotional and/or sexual exclusivity. It covers incidence statistics from surveys such as the Kinsey Reports, the General Social Survey and the National Health and Social Life Survey, gender and sexual-orientation differences in jealousy, and the emotional responses and outcomes for partners. It also surveys causes, cultural and anthropological views, and evolutionary and strategic theories that try to explain infidelity; the note is truncated mid-list in its discussion of jealousy's defensive functions.
one_line: Overview of infidelity covering its definition, prevalence statistics, gender and orientation differences, consequences, causes, and evolutionary and cultural explanations.
key_facts: Infidelity is defined as a violation of a couple's emotional and/or sexual exclusivity that commonly results in anger, sexual jealousy, and rivalry.
The Kinsey Reports in the early 1950s found that around half of men and a quarter of women studied had committed adultery.
The General Social Survey at the University of Chicago has interviewed people in monogamous relationships since 1972, finding about 12% of men and 7% of women admit to an extramarital relationship.
A University of Washington, Seattle study of 19,065 people over 15 years found men's infidelity rates rose from 20% to 28%.
The National Health and Social Life Survey found 4% of married men, 16% of cohabiting men and 37% of dating men engaged in sexual infidelity in the previous year.
Paternal discrepancy estimates in the media of as high as 30% were traced by sociologist Michael Gilding to an informal remark at a 1972 conference.
Paternal discrepancy is generally 1–2% among European samples and less than 2% in the sampled Middle Eastern population.

Men are theorized to be 60% more likely to be disturbed by sexual infidelity, whereas women are 83% more likely to be disturbed by emotional infidelity, according to proponents of an innate sex difference.
C. F. Harris's meta-analysis found sex differences in jealousy were almost exclusively found in forced-choice studies.
Harris (2002) tested 210 individuals, including 48 homosexual women, 50 homosexual men, 40 heterosexual women and 49 heterosexual men.
Charney and Parnass (1995) report negative reactions to infidelity including rage, loss of trust, depression, damaged self-esteem and fear of abandonment.
Another study reported that nearly 60% of partners who were cheated on had emotional problems and depression following disclosure of the affair.
Schneider et al. (1999) reported that even though 60% of participants initially threatened to leave, a threat to leave did not actually predict the eventual outcome.
Anthropologist Bobbi Low says humans are "slightly polygamous", while Deborah Blum believes we are "ambiguously monogamous".
Strategic pluralism theory holds that promiscuity and infidelity are more common in environments with little stress and threat to offspring viability.
David Schmitt (2001) surveyed 16,964 individuals in 53 countries and found mate poaching happens significantly more frequently in Middle Eastern countries such as Turkey and Lebanon.
